senses.definition: To back a claim with evidence that someone else can check.
senses.caution: Asking someone to substantiate a claim shows you doubt it. For a colleague's claim in front of their boss, just ask for the source instead.
senses.example: I can substantiate the thirty per cent figure from two quarters of tickets, it is not a vendor number.

cues.text: A director accepts your recommendation and then asks where the number came from, and you want the verb for supplying that.
You are reviewing a paper whose central claim rests on one unsourced statistic, and you want a polite verb for what the authors still have to do to that claim.
A friend repeats a health claim they read online, and you want the verb for what they would need to do with evidence before you believe it.
An insurer asks you to back the value of a lost item with something more than your word for it.

distractors: To repeat a claim until people accept it.
To state something plainly and without hedging.
To write down what was decided so it can be found later.
To argue a case on behalf of somebody who is not in the room.
To take an existing figure and adjust it for inflation over time.

gloss_distractors: known only to a few people
senses.definition: Large enough to matter, said of an amount or a change without giving a number.
senses.caution: People will ask how much, so give the number if you have it. Use the word alone only when you are not allowed to share the figure.
senses.example: There is a substantial gap between what the pilot proved and what the rollout is assuming.

cues.text: You want to call the cost reduction meaningful in a paper where you are not allowed to publish the exact figure.
A colleague's contribution to the project went far beyond a review, and you want to credit it in writing.
Describing a restaurant to a friend, you want a word for portions that genuinely fill you rather than decorate the plate.
A neighbour asks what the roof repair cost, and you want to convey that it was a lot without naming the figure.

distractors: Small enough to ignore for now.
Measured precisely and reported to two decimal places.
Growing steadily but from a very small starting point.
Set aside in a budget for costs that have not yet been identified in any detail.
Counted twice by mistake because two systems both reported the same transaction.
